Title: A Survey of Agentic GraphRAG: From Retrieval-augmented Generation to Graph-native Agents
Summary: This survey provides a comprehensive analysis of Agentic GraphRAG, an emerging paradigm that integrates Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Agentic RAG. While large language models know a lot, their knowledge is frozen at training time and they often suffer from hallucinations. RAG is the standard workaround: before the model answers, fetch relevant text from an external corpus and generate response based on the it. Two lines of work have pushed RAG in different directions: (1) GraphRAG changes what the model retrieves from: instead of a pile of text chunks indexed by similarity, it builds a knowledge graph of entities and their relations, summarizes densely connected regions, and retrieves over that. (2) Agentic RAG changes how retrieval happens: moving beyond one shot generation based on user query, an agent plans, acts, critiques its own work, keeps memory across steps, and then retrieves multiple times as needed. Recent work combines the two, with Karpathy's LLM Wiki as a salient example of non-tech-savvy solutions. The agent's planning, acting, critiquing, and remembering all operate over graph operations. The graph stops being a passive lookup table and becomes the space the agent moves through. This survey treats such combination as a research area in its own right. We organize recent primary papers on a 4x3 grid (four agent roles vs. three graph operations) grounded in a central observation: pure GraphRAG and standalone Agentic RAG each possess recurring failure modes, and the combination of the two paradigms can effectively mitigate these. The body of the survey covers seven method families that populate the grid: single-agent iterative traversal, self-evolving GraphRAG, RL-trained graph walkers, multi-agent graph systems, agentic graph construction, persistent graph memory, and hybrid structured–unstructured retrieval. Three application areas ground the discussion: medicine, legal reasoning, and cyber threat intelligence. Furthermore, recent papers reach directly opposing conclusions about whether graphs are still needed once an agent is in the loop. We trace where the disagreement comes from, and discuss evaluation protocols that jointly score agent trajectories and retrievals, alongside the adversarial robustness of agent–graph systems.

Title: Metode Retrieval-Augmented Generation dalam Pengembangan Chatbot Large Language Model pada Service Informasi Publik Disdukcapil Anambas
Summary: Layanan administrasi kependudukan di Kabupaten Kepulauan Anambas menghadapi tantangan besar terkait keterbatasan akses informasi yang disebabkan oleh kondisi geografis. Informasi layanan pada website resmi Disdukcapil yang bersifat pasif seringkali menyulitkan masyarakat untuk memperoleh jawaban yang cepat dan relevan. Kondisi ini berakibat pada penumpukan antrean layanan dan berpotensi menurunkan kepuasan publik. Sebagai solusi, sebuah aplikasi chatbot cerdas berbasis Large Language Model (LLM) dengan pendekatan Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) telah dikembangkan. Metode ini secara efektif menggabungkan kemampuan pencarian informasi presisi dari basis data dokumen dengan kemampuan LLM dalam memahami bahasa alami untuk menghasilkan jawaban kontekstual. Proses pengembangan sistem ini dilakukan menggunakan framework LangChain, vector store ChromaDB, dan diintegrasikan ke antarmuka web sebagai frontend. Informasi layanan resmi Disdukcapil diproses melalui tahapan chunking, embedding, hingga pembuatan pipeline RAG. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa chatbot mampu merespons pertanyaan layanan kependudukan secara akurat dan efisien. Berdasarkan evaluasi menggunakan metrik BERTScore, sistem memperoleh rata-rata skor Precision sebesar 98,5%, Recall sebesar 99,1%, dan F1-Score sebesar 98,8%. Sistem ini dapat diakses dari mana saja, sangat membantu masyarakat di wilayah terpencil, dan menjadi prototipe awal yang potensial untuk mendukung digitalisasi pelayanan publik di daerah kepulauan.

The paper contributes a bounded design-science foundation for future inter-rater reliability testing, Delphi expert validation, organizational pilots, psychometric evaluation, and dashboard usability assessment.

Title: A Survey of Agentic GraphRAG: From Retrieval-augmented Generation to Graph-native Agents
Summary: This survey provides a comprehensive analysis of Agentic GraphRAG, an emerging paradigm that integrates Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Agentic RAG. While large language models know a lot, their knowledge is frozen at training time and they often suffer from hallucinations. RAG is the standard workaround: before the model answers, fetch relevant text from an external corpus and generate response based on the it. Two lines of work have pushed RAG in different directions: (1) GraphRAG changes what the model retrieves from: instead of a pile of text chunks indexed by similarity, it builds a knowledge graph of entities and their relations, summarizes densely connected regions, and retrieves over that. (2) Agentic RAG changes how retrieval happens: moving beyond one shot generation based on user query, an agent plans, acts, critiques its own work, keeps memory across steps, and then retrieves multiple times as needed. Recent work combines the two, with Karpathy's LLM Wiki as a salient example of non-tech-savvy solutions. The agent's planning, acting, critiquing, and remembering all operate over graph operations. The graph stops being a passive lookup table and becomes the space the agent moves through. This survey treats such combination as a research area in its own right. We organize recent primary papers on a 4x3 grid (four agent roles vs. three graph operations) grounded in a central observation: pure GraphRAG and standalone Agentic RAG each possess recurring failure modes, and the combination of the two paradigms can effectively mitigate these. The body of the survey covers seven method families that populate the grid: single-agent iterative traversal, self-evolving GraphRAG, RL-trained graph walkers, multi-agent graph systems, agentic graph construction, persistent graph memory, and hybrid structured–unstructured retrieval. Three application areas ground the discussion: medicine, legal reasoning, and cyber threat intelligence. Furthermore, recent papers reach directly opposing conclusions about whether graphs are still needed once an agent is in the loop. We trace where the disagreement comes from, and discuss evaluation protocols that jointly score agent trajectories and retrievals, alongside the adversarial robustness of agent–graph systems.
